item.text: I’ll read the five note parts in order, group the answers by question, write the map, then run the required check.

item.aggregated_output:
<<2:175 notes, part 0 of 0..4>>
[MUJAHID:v1p94#3/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | He reads فما أصبرهم on the pattern of amazement: how well they act in falsehood.
[MUQATIL:2:174-176/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | They exchanged their prior faith in Muhammad for denial after his mission and chose punishment over forgiveness; their evil acts make them endure the Fire.
[FARRA:v1p102#2/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | One reading takes the phrase as asking what made them endure the Fire.
[FARRA:v1p102#2/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · author | reports | The other reading is “how bold they are toward the Fire”; the judge's reported idiom ما أصبرك على الله supports this sense.
[MAJAZ:v1p64/r4] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | ما is relative here: “what made them endure the Fire and called them to it”; this is not an exclamation.
[ABDURRAZZAQ:v1p66/r1] ABDURRAZZAQ, d. 211 · قتادة | reports | Qatada explains the question ‘How patient they are toward the Fire!’ as meaning how audacious they are in facing it.
[AKHFASH:v1p166/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · some | reports | Some take فما أصبرهم على النار as an exclamation of astonishment at them, like قتل الإنسان ما أكفره. | mentions 80:17
[AKHFASH:v1p166/r5] AKHFASH, d. 215 · some | reports | Others read it as a question: what makes them endure the Fire, or what is it that makes them endure it?
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p69#2/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | ما أصبرهم means “how bold they are toward the Fire.”
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p69#2/r2] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī relays a judge's idiom ما أصبرك على الله, said to a man who swore away another's right, as evidence for “how bold.”
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p69#2/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · مجاهد | prefers | Mujāhid's “how capable they are of the deeds of the people of the Fire” is a good reading, with deeds omitted and endurance understood.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p69#2/r4] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda takes ما as “what thing made them endure the Fire and brought them to it,” not as an exclamation.
[TUSTARI:2:175/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · سهل | reports | “How patient they are on the Fire” means they dare issue religious judgments without knowledge of the Sunna or law and perform the deeds of Hell's people.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | The phrase means how brazen they are to perform deeds that bring them near the Fire.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الحسن | reports | They have no patience for the Fire; the phrase instead marvels at how daring they are toward it.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد أو سعيد بن جبير أو بعض أصحابه | reports | The phrase means how brazen they are toward the Fire.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · الربيع بن أنس | reports | They are daring and seemingly patient toward the Fire.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Another interpretation says they are practiced in falsehood and wrongdoing.
[TAB-FULL:v3p67#3/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · السدي | reports | The particle ma is interrogative: what could make them endure the Fire?
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عطاء | reports | A question asks what makes them endure the Fire after abandoning truth and following falsehood.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو بكر بن عياش | reports | He reads the clause as a question, arguing that a statement about patience would have a different case ending.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | The question asks what made them persist in the Fire and dare to act as they did.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد، الحسن، قتادة | reports | Another view treats the words as an exclamation at their audacity in doing the deeds of those destined for the Fire.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid also explains the phrase as asking how skilled they are at the deeds of the Fire’s people.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers the exclamation that they are brazen toward the Fire and expert in its people’s deeds; Arabic uses this construction for audacity, and Fire stands for its punishment.
[TAB-FULL:v3p70/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The wonder concerns scholars who concealed Muhammad’s prophethood for bribes despite knowing this would earn God’s anger; mentioning Fire stands for its punishment, as comparisons to Hatim and Antara omit the repeated quality. | mentions 80:17
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | Some interpret God’s not speaking to them as a sign of anger, as when one says a person refuses to speak to someone because he is angry.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | Another explanation is that God sends no angels to greet them; a further possibility is that He does not let them hear His speech, unlike the righteous.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | ولا يزكيهم means God does not praise them; one whom God does not praise is punished.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | أليم means painful, with مؤلم describing an intensified degree of pain.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | One reading of فما أصبرهم is ‘what makes them so patient with the Fire?’
[ZAJJAJ:v1p245/r6] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعضهم | reports | Another reading asks what makes them endure deeds leading to the Fire, though they know opposing the Prophet leads there; ‘what makes him patient against hunger?’ has the same idiom.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p286/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو العالية | reports | They chose error over guidance and punishment over forgiveness; Qatada and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas report the same interpretation.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p286/r2] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · أبو العالية | reports | The exclamation about their endurance means they are remarkably patient and bold in doing the deeds of the people of Hell; several early authorities agree.
[IBNABIHATIM:v1p286/r3] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid instead explains the exclamation as how knowledgeable they are about the deeds of the people of Hell.
[BAQILLANI:v1p78/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Qur'an uses the same vivid personifying mode as poetic images of a corner kissing a footprint and a minbar walking toward its addressee; Hell is shown speaking, seeing, and nearly bursting with rage. | mentions 50:30, 25:12, 67:8
[BAQILLANI:v1p78/r2] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Baqillani calls mumathalah, which Qudama names tamthil, a metaphorical figure opposite irdaf: it compresses an allusion by choosing words that themselves exemplify the intended meaning; this verse is an example.
[BAQILLANI:v1p78/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · الخليل بن أحمد والأصمعي وعبد الله بن المعتز | reports | Most authorities define mutabaqa as mentioning a thing together with its opposite, such as night and day or black and white; al-Khalil, al-Asma'i, and Ibn al-Mu'tazz hold this account.
[THALABI:v2p47/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الكسائي وقطرب | reports | They interpret it as how steadfast the people are in the deeds of Hell's inhabitants, like comparing generosity to Hatim's.
[THALABI:v2p47/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · مجاهد | reports | He reads it as sarcasm: how knowledgeable they are about the deeds of Hell's people.
[THALABI:v2p47/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Another exclamation means how long God will keep them in the Fire, like asking how long someone bears beating or imprisonment.
[THALABI:v2p47/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء والسدي وابن زيد وأبو بكر بن عباس | reports | They take ma as an interrogative: what made them endure Hell when they abandoned truth and followed falsehood? The question expresses contempt.
[THALABI:v2p47/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | They exchanged misguidance for guidance and punishment for forgiveness.
[THALABI:v2p47/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن وقتادة والربيع | reports | For the exclamation reading, they say the verse does not mean the people endure Hell patiently but that they dare to do deeds leading to it; this is Yemeni usage.
[THALABI:v2p47/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · قاضي اليمن | reports | A Yemeni judge used the phrase how patient are you with God to mean how daring are you against Him, supporting the boldness interpretation.
[THALABI:v2p47/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · المورج | reports | The meaning is how persistent they are in deeds that lead to Hell; they had knowledge, and opposing the Prophet makes a person of Hell.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p223#3/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may mean how long He keeps them in the Fire, using ṣabara for keeping someone confined.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p223#3/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The phrase may be an astonished question: what could make them endure the Fire?
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p223#3/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The people meant are the previously mentioned Jewish scholars, who exchanged unbelief for faith and Hell for Paradise.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p223#3/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبو صالح | reports | “How patient they are with the Fire!” means how daring they are toward it.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p223#3/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | It may mean how steadfastly they pursue deeds that lead them to the Fire.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p506#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The fa answers the preceding description: those who traded guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment are, by implication, astonishingly patient toward the Fire.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p506#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل التأويل | reports | One reported interpretation makes mā exclamatory; the author parses it as a subject, aḥsana as a past-tense verb and predicate, and Zaydan as its object.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p506#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Mā is chosen for exclamation because its ambiguity points to the surprising thing; shayʾ could imply belittling it or report a settled fact, whereas an exclamation startles the hearer.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p506#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Excl

amative aḥsana is a triliteral verb shifted to a quadriliteral form; its fixed final fatḥa shows it is verbal, and the object is accusative because the thing is truly acted upon.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v3p506#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The diminutive mā aḥaysana in poetry does not make the exclamative a noun; it only imitates nouns while remaining a verb.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:174-175/r2] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They exchanged guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment by rejecting Muhammad’s message and concealing his description.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:174-175/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | “How patient they are with fire” asks what drove them to it by abandoning truth for falsehood; it is a rebuke.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:174-175/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · قيل | reports | An alternative reading is “How audacious they are toward the Fire!”
[DAMGHANI:v1p263/r1] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Dāmghānī explains ishtirāʾ as purchase; in the cited 9:111 image, believers have sold themselves to God. | mentions 9:111
[DAMGHANI:v1p271/r9] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Aṣbar in this phrase expresses boldness: how brazenly they act toward the Fire.
[JISHUMI:v1p485/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The verse indicates that unbelief is their own act, refuting the Jabriyya.
[JISHUMI:v1p485/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Cursing and punishment are deserved through the agent's actions.
[JISHUMI:v1p485/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | A sin committed knowingly is graver, and its perpetrator receives a harsher punishment.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p185/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · عطاء والسدي | reports | They take fa-mā aṣbarahum as a question: what has made them endure the Fire after abandoning truth for falsehood?
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p185/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | They say the phrase means how brazen they are in doing deeds that bring them toward the Fire; they have no actual patience for it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p185/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الكسائي | reports | He reads it as asking how persistently they continue doing the deeds of the people of the Fire.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p241#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Choosing misguidance after rejecting accessible guidance is pictured as trade; punishment follows the chosen error and forgiveness would have followed the guidance they discarded, so both are included in the metaphorical purchase.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p241#2/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · جمهور المفسرين | reports | Most exegetes take mā aṣbarahum as an exclamation: they are astonishingly fit to remain long in the Fire, as in 80:17 and 19:38. | mentions 80:17, 19:38
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p241#2/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · قتادة والحسن وابن جبير والربيع | reports | They explain the exclamation as amazement at the hypocrites' audacity: their behavior shows they have prepared themselves for the Fire and are willing to enter it.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p241#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · معمر بن المثنى | reports | Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā reads mā as an interrogative: what has made them endure the Fire? Ibn ʿAṭiyya considers the exclamatory reading clearer.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p241#2/r5] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Aṣbara can mean commanding someone to be patient or making someone patient; either sense works if the clause is interrogative.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p242/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad calls the phrase an interrogative report, not an exclamation, and parses aṣbara as “confined or forced,” citing the prohibition on tormenting a living creature and a poetic line.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p242/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · القاضي أبو محمد | rejects | Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-Mubarrad's vowel analysis is wrong: the poetic form is aṣbarahā with fatḥa on hamza and ḍamma on bāʾ, past tense of ṣabara; this undercuts the proposed “make patient” sense.
[TABRISI:2:175/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | ما أصبرهم may be an exclamation like the wording in 80:17, meaning they have become an object of astonishment; an Arab saying likewise describes one as patient toward God's punishment. | mentions 80:17
[TABRISI:2:175/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · الكسائي وقطرب | reports | Al-Kisāʾī and Quṭrub read it as how persistent they are in deeds leading to the Fire.
[TABRISI:2:175/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās takes the wording as an actual question: what keeps them confined to the Fire?
[TABRISI:2:175/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Literal divine astonishment is impossible because God knows everything; the exclamation instead makes the unbelievers an object of human amazement, rebuke, and reproach, while the readings can also be understood interrogatively.
[TABRISI:2:175/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad calls the interrogative reading a good rebuke that makes people marvel at those who freely bring ruin on themselves.
[TABRISI:2:175/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Alternatively, the phrase asks what makes them endure the Fire; the verb can mean to subject someone to what they dislike, as in al-Ḥuṭayʾa's poem.
[TABRISI:2:175/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The verse refers back to those who traded misguidance for guidance, replacing belief in the Prophet with unbelief.
[TABRISI:2:175/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Other interpretations take misguidance as concealing what they knew about the Prophet, or as punishment exchanged for reward and Paradise.
[TABRISI:2:175/r5] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو مسلم | reports | Abū Muslim considers “exchanging punishment for forgiveness” a reinforcement of the preceding exchange.
[TABRISI:2:175/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · القاضي | prefers | Al-Qāḍī says they knowingly exchanged forgiveness for punishment by persisting in disobedience; al-Ṭabrisī prefers this because it adds a distinct meaning.
[TABRISI:2:175/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda take فما أصبرهم as “how audacious they are toward the Fire.”
[TABRISI:2:175/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · مجاهد | reports | Mujāhid interprets it as “how active they are in deeds of the people of the Fire.”
[TABRISI:2:175/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj understands the phrase as how long they remain in the Fire, like asking how long someone can endure prison.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Ṣabr is restraining the self from what it is drawn toward; Ramadan is called the month of patience, and any restraint can be described as ṣabr.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | A tied animal used as a target and shot until killed is called المصبورة; this practice is prohibited.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r3] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | Someone patient through calamity is called ṣābir because he restrains himself from panic.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari transmits an explanation that patience is named for its bitterness in the heart, like the bitterness of ṣabr in the mouth.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | The most common Qur'anic sense is patience itself, or restraining the self; examples are given in 3:17, 14:21, and 38:44. | mentions 3:17, 14:21, 38:44
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · بعض المفسرين | reports | A second Qur'anic sense is fasting, illustrated by the command to seek help through patience and prayer. | mentions 2:45
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ interprets فما أصبرهم على النار as an expression of how daring they are toward the Fire.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p387/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī reports a Bedouin's rebuke to a liar, ما أصبرك على الله, meaning how audacious you are toward God.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The buyers chose misguidance over guidance.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عكرمة | reports | ʿIkrima and al-Rabiʿ explain “how patient they are” as patience in deeds that lead them to the Fire.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan and Mujahid take the phrase to mean how bold they are to face the Fire; al-Kisaʾi cites an Arab’s “How bold you are before God!”
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj reads it as asking how long they will remain in the Fire, as in asking how long someone endures imprisonment.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن الأنباري | reports | Ibn al-Anbari says it asks what has made them endure the Fire.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · عطاء | reports | One grammatical view makes mā interrogative—“what made them patient?”—reported from ʿAta, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, and others.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | reports | The alternative makes mā exclamatory, like “how excellent Zayd is”; Ibn al-Anbari says the exclamation is attributed to God to make creatures marvel, not because God marvels as they do.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p176#3/r8] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The verse explains their behavior by saying God sent the Book in truth and those who differed about it are in deep division. | mentions 2:176
[RAZI-FULL:v5p25#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In this life knowledge and guidance are best, while ignorance and error are worst; in the next, forgiveness is best and punishment worst, so the concealters are greatest losers in both worlds.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p25#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the Jewish scholars knew the truth, the reward for disclosing it, and the punishment for hiding it and spreading doubt, their concealment amounts to exchanging forgiveness for punishment.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p25#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عطاء وابن زيد | reports | One reading takes the phrase as a rebuking question: what makes them endure the Fire by abandoning t

ruth for falsehood? Ibn al-Anbari notes that af‘ala can mean fa‘ala.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p25#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The other reading is an exclamation: knowingly choosing what entails Hell makes them act as if they accept and endure its consequence; the description concerns their present life of moral responsibility.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p25#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأصم | reports | Al-Asamm says the phrase describes their future silence when ordered to remain in Hell; Razi rejects this as shifting a present description into the future and because the damned may cry out and plead. | mentions 23:108
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | reports | The fifth argument begins by saying a quality belongs to a thing either intrinsically or through another cause, a premise for rejecting the proposed paraphrase of the exclamation.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | They argue that an indefinite noun cannot serve as the subject, so the Basran analysis wrongly makes the most indefinite word a subject.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | If “How good Zayd is!” meant “something made Zayd good,” the plain statement should retain the exclamation, but it does not.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | If God is the one who made Zayd, the sun, moon, and world good, He should be referred to by “who,” not “what”; yet “who made Zayd good” is not an exclamation.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | The Basran parsing would make “How good Zayd is!” no different from an ordinary clause such as “Zayd struck Amr,” which has no exclamatory force.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | Knowledge that something made Zayd good is necessary, while recognizing an object of wonder is not; thus the proposed paraphrase lacks the exclamation’s meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | Their analogy with “a man is writer” is uninformative: everyone knows that some man writes and some cause made Zayd good, so the sentence adds nothing.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكوفيون | rejects | The diminutive associated with nouns occurs with ma af‘alahu; if such forms are incompatible with verbs, the formula is not verbal, but if compatible, diminutives should apply to verbs generally, which they do not.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Wonder ordinarily combines magnification with an unclear cause, but the word can express magnification alone; divine wonder means magnification, unlike human wonder that involves an unknown cause.
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · شريح | reports | Shurayh rejected the damma reading “I wonder” in 37:12 because ignorance of a cause cannot be attributed to God. | mentions 37:12
[RAZI-FULL:v5p26/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النخعي | reports | Al-Nakha‘i says divine wonder means sheer magnification; similarly, divine laughter, mockery, and cunning do not have the human meanings of those terms.

item.text: The notes so far give several readings of “فما أصبرهم”: audacity, persistence in deeds, a rebuking question, and endurance in the Fire. I’ll keep those answers distinct and attach each source’s evidence to its position.
